{{Short description|Mathematical theorem}}
In [[mathematics]], '''Ramanujan's master theorem''', named after [[Srinivasa Ramanujan]],{{sfn|Berndt|1985}} is a technique that provides an analytic expression for the [[Mellin transform]] of an [[analytic function]].
[[File:Ramanujan's "Master Theorem" page.jpg|thumb|Page from Ramanujan's notebook stating his Master theorem.]]

The result is stated as follows:

If a complex-valued function <math display="inline"> f(x) </math> has an expansion of the form <math display=block>f(x)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{\,\varphi(k)\,}{k!}(-x)^k  </math> 

where <math display="inline">\varphi(s)</math> is an analytic function, then the [[Mellin transform]] of <math display="inline">f(x)</math> is given by

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty x^{s-1} f(x) \, dx = \Gamma(s)\,\varphi(-s) </math>

where <math display="inline">\Gamma(s)</math> is the [[gamma function]].

It was widely used by Ramanujan to calculate definite integrals and [[infinite series]].

Higher-dimensional versions of this theorem also appear in [[quantum physics]] through [[Feynman diagram]]s.{{sfn|González|Moll|Schmidt|2011}}

A similar result was also obtained by [[J. W. L. Glaisher|Glaisher]].{{sfn|Glaisher|1874||pp=53–55}}
== Alternative formalism ==
An alternative formulation of Ramanujan's master theorem is as follows:

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty  x^{s-1}\left(\,\lambda(0) - x\,\lambda(1) + x^2\,\lambda(2) -\,\cdots\,\right) dx = \frac{\pi}{\,\sin(\pi s)\,}\,\lambda(-s) </math>

which gets converted to the above form after substituting <math display="inline">\lambda(n) \equiv \frac{\varphi(n)}{\,\Gamma(1+n)\,} </math> and using the functional equation for the [[gamma function]].

The integral above is convergent for <math display="inline"> 0 < \operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(s) < 1 </math> subject to growth conditions on <math display="inline"> \varphi </math>.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|pp=103-120}} 

== Proof ==
A proof subject to "natural" assumptions (though not the weakest necessary conditions) to Ramanujan's master theorem was provided by [[G. H. Hardy]]{{sfn|Hardy|1978}}(chapter XI) employing the [[residue theorem]] and the well-known [[Mellin inversion theorem]].
{{Collapse top|title=Ramanujan's proof of his master theorem{{sfn|Berndt|1985}}}}

Recall Euler's representation of the Gamma function <math>\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}e^{-mx}dx=m^{-n}\Gamma(n)</math>

choosing <math>m=r^k</math>, multiplying both sides by <math>\frac{f^{k}(a)h^k}{k!}</math> and then summing over <math>0\le k</math> to obtain:
<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{f^{k}(a)h^k}{k!}\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}e^{-r^kx}dx=\Gamma(n)\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{f^{k}(a)(hr^{-n})^k}{k!}</math>

Observing the sum in the RHS is a Taylor Series and writing <math>e^{-r^kx}</math> in its series expansion:

<math>\sum_{k=0}^\infty\frac{f^{k}(a)h^k}{k!}\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{(-r^kx)^j}{j!}dx=\Gamma(n)f(hr^{-n}+a)</math>

Rewriting the LHS:

<math>\sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^j}{j!}\int_0^\infty x^{n-1+j} \sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{f^k(a)(hr^j)^k}{k!}dx=\Gamma(n)f(hr^{-n}+a)</math>

Then once again observing the sum over <math>k</math> is a Taylor series:
<math>\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}\sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{f^{k}(hr^j+a)(-x)^j}{j!}dx=\Gamma(n)f(hr^{-n}+a)</math>

Finally defining <math>f(hr^{N}+a)= \phi(N)</math> and letting <math>F(x)=\sum_{j=0}^\infty \frac{\phi(j)(-x)^j}{j!}</math> we gain the master theorem:
<math>\int_0^\infty x^{n-1}F(x)dx=\Gamma(n)\phi(-n)</math>
{{Collapse bottom}}

{{Collapse top|title=Hardy's proof of the master theorem{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=4|loc=Thm. 3.2}} }}
Let <math>\lambda(z)</math> be an analytic single-valued function defined on a half plane 

<math>H(\delta) = \left\{z\in \mathbb{C} : \mathfrak{R}(z)\ge - \delta \right\} </math>

for some <math>0 < \delta < 1</math>. Suppose that, for some <math>A< \pi</math>, <math>\lambda</math> satisfies the growth condition

<math>|\lambda(v+iw)|<Ce^{Pv+A|w|}</math>

for all <math>z=v+iw \in H(\delta)</math>. Let <math>0<x<e^{-P}</math>. This implies the series <math>F(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty (-x)^n\lambda(n)</math> converges. Observing <math>\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi s)}</math> has poles at <math>s \in \mathbb{Z}^-</math> with residue <math>(-1)^{-s}</math>, application of the residue theorem yields
  
<math>F(x)=\frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{c-i\infty}^{c+i\infty}\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi s)}\lambda(-s)x^{-s}ds</math>

for any <math>0<c<\delta</math>. This integral converges absolutely and uniformly for <math>c\in(a,b)</math> for any <math>0<a,b<\delta</math>. Applying the Mellin inversion theorem yields

<math>\int_0^\infty x^{s-1}F(x)dx=\frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi s)}\lambda(-s)</math>
{{Collapse bottom}}

== Application to Bernoulli polynomials ==
The [[generating function]] of the [[Bernoulli polynomials]] <math display="inline">B_k(x)</math> is given by:

<math display=block>  \frac{z\,e^{x\,z}}{\,e^z - 1\,}=\sum_{k=0}^\infty B_k(x)\,\frac{z^k}{k!} </math>

These polynomials are given in terms of the [[Hurwitz zeta function]]:

<math display=block>  \zeta(s,a) = \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{1}{\,(n+a)^s\,} </math>

by <math display="inline">\zeta(1-n,a) = -\frac{B_n(a)}{n}</math> for <math display="inline">~ n \geq 1 </math>.
Using the Ramanujan master theorem and the generating function of Bernoulli polynomials one has the following integral representation:{{sfn|Espinosa|Moll|2002|pp=449–468}}

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty  x^{s-1}\left(\frac{e^{-ax}}{\,1 - e^{-x}\,}-\frac{1}{x}\right) dx = \Gamma(s)\,\zeta(s,a) \!</math>

which is valid for <math display="inline"> 0 < \operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(s) < 1</math>.

== Application to the gamma function ==
Weierstrass's definition of the gamma function

<math display=block>  \Gamma(x) = \frac{\,e^{-\gamma\,x\,}}{x}\,\prod_{n=1}^\infty \left(\,1 + \frac{x}{n}\,\right)^{-1} e^{x/n} \!</math>

is equivalent to expression

<math display=block>  \log\Gamma(1+x) = -\gamma\,x + \sum_{k=2}^\infty \frac{\,\zeta(k)\,}{k}\,(-x)^k </math>

where <math display="inline">\zeta(k)</math> is the [[Riemann zeta function]].

Then applying Ramanujan master theorem we have:

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty x^{s-1} \frac{\,\gamma\,x + \log\Gamma(1+x)\,}{x^2} \mathrm d x =  \frac{\pi}{\sin(\pi s)}\frac{\zeta(2-s)}{2-s} \!</math>

valid for <math display="inline"> 0 < \operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(s) < 1 </math>.

Special cases of <math display="inline">s = \frac{1}{2} </math> and <math display="inline"> s = \frac{3}{4} </math> are

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty \frac{\,\gamma x+\log\Gamma(1+x)\,}{x^{5/2}} \, \mathrm d x = \frac{2\pi}{3}\,\zeta\left( \frac{3}{2} \right) </math>

<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty \frac{\,\gamma\,x+\log\Gamma(1+x)\,}{x^{9/4}} \, \mathrm d x = \sqrt{2} \frac{4\pi}{5} \zeta\left(\frac 5 4\right) </math>

== Application to Bessel functions ==
The [[Bessel function]] of the first kind has the [[power series]]
<math display=block>  J_\nu(z)=\sum_{k=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^k}{\Gamma(k+\nu+1)k!}\bigg(\frac{z}{2}\bigg)^{2k+\nu} </math>

By Ramanujan's master theorem, together with some identities for the gamma function and rearranging, we can evaluate the integral

<math display=block>  \frac{2^{\nu-2s}\pi}{\sin{(\pi(s-\nu))}} \int_0^\infty z^{s-1-\nu/2}J_\nu(\sqrt{z})\,dz = \Gamma(s)\Gamma(s-\nu)</math>

valid for <math display="inline">0 < 2\operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(s) < \operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(\nu)+\tfrac{3}{2} </math>.

Equivalently, if the [[spherical Bessel function]] <math display="inline">j_\nu(z) </math> is preferred, the formula becomes

<math display=block>  \frac{2^{\nu-2s}\sqrt{\pi}(1-2s+2\nu)}{\cos{(\pi(s-\nu))}} \int_0^\infty z^{s-1-\nu/2}j_\nu(\sqrt{z})\,dz = \Gamma(s)\Gamma\bigg(\frac{1}{2}+s-\nu\bigg)</math>

valid for <math display="inline"> 0 < 2\operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(s) < \operatorname{\mathcal{Re}}(\nu)+2 </math>.

The solution is remarkable in that it is able to interpolate across the major identities for the gamma function.  In particular, the choice of <math display="inline">J_{1/2}(\sqrt z) </math> gives the square of the gamma function, <math display="inline">j_0(\sqrt{z})</math> gives the [[duplication formula]], <math display="inline">z^{-1/2}J_{1}(\sqrt z)</math> gives the [[reflection formula]], and fixing to the evaluable <math display="inline">s=\frac{1}{2}</math> or <math display="inline">s=1</math> gives the gamma function by itself, up to reflection and scaling.

== Bracket integration method ==  
The bracket integration method (method of brackets) applies Ramanujan's master theorem to a broad range of integrals.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Moll|2010|pp=50-73}}  The bracket integration method generates the integrand's [[series expansion]], creates a bracket series, identifies the series [[coefficient]] and [[formula]] [[parameter]]s and computes the integral.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Jiu|Moll|2020|pp=983-985}}
===Integration formulas===
This section identifies the integration formulas for [[Integral|integrands]] with and without consecutive [[integer]] exponents and for single and double integrals.  The integration formula for double integrals may be generalized to any [[multiple integral]].  In all cases, there is a parameter value <math display="inline">n^{\ast}</math> or array of parameter values <math display="inline">N^{\ast}</math> that solves one or more [[linear equation]]s derived from the [[Exponentiation|exponent]] terms of the integrand's series expansion. 
====Consecutive integer exponents, 1 variable====
This is the [[function series]] expansion, integral and integration formula for an integral whose integrand's series expansion contains consecutive integer exponents.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=117|loc=Eqn. 9.5}}      
<math display=block> \begin{align} 
&f(y)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!} \ \varphi(n) \ y^{n} \\
&\int_0^\infty y^{c-1} f(y) \, dy \\
&= \int_0^\infty \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!} \ \varphi(n) \ y^{n+c-1} dy \\
&=\Gamma(-n^{\ast})\,\varphi(n^{\ast}). 
\end{align}</math>
The parameter <math>n^{\ast}</math> is a solution to this linear equation.
<math display=block> n^{\ast}+c=0, \ n^{\ast}= -c</math>
====General exponents, 1 variable====
Applying the substitution <math display="inline">y=x^{a}</math> generates the function series expansion, integral and integration formula for an integral whose integrand's series expansion may not contain consecutive integer exponents.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Jiu|Moll|2020|pp=983-985}}
<math display=block> \begin{align} 
&f(x)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!} \ \varphi(n) \ x^{an} \\
&\int_0^\infty x^{c-1} f(x) \, dx \\
&=\int_0^\infty \sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n}}{n!} \ \varphi(n) \ x^{an+c-1} dx \\
&=a^{-1} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast})\,\varphi(n^{\ast}). \\
\end{align}</math>
The parameter <math display="inline">n^{\ast}</math> is a solution to this linear equation.
<math display=block> a \ n^{\ast}+c=0, \ n^{\ast}=-a^{-1} c </math>
====Consecutive integer exponents, double integral====
This is the function series expansion, integral and integration formula for a double integral whose integrand's series expansion contains consecutive integer exponents.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=118}}
<math display=block> \begin{align} &f(y_{1},y_{2})=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(-1)^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!} \frac{(-1)^{n_{2}}}{n_{2}!}   \ \varphi(n_{1},n_{2}) \ y_{1}^{n_{1}}  \ y_{2}^{n_{2}} \\
&\int_0^\infty y^{c_{1}-1}_{1} y^{c_{2}-1}_{2} \ f(y_{1},y_{2}) \ dy_{1} \ dy_{2} \\
&=\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \sum^\infty_{n_{1}=0} \sum^\infty_{n_{2}=0} \frac{(-1)^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!} \frac{(-1)^{n_{2}}}{n_{2}!}  \ \varphi(n_{1},n_{2}) \ y_{1}^{n_{1}+c_{1}-1}  \ y_{2}^{n_{2}+c_{2}-1} \ dy_{1} \ dy_{2} \\
&=\Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{2}) \ \varphi(n^{\ast}_{1},n^{\ast}_{2}). \\
\end{align}</math> 
The parameters <math display="inline">n^{\ast}_{1}</math> and <math display="inline">n^{\ast}_{2}</math> are solutions to these linear equations.
<math display=block> n^{\ast}_{1}+c_{1}=0, \ n^{\ast}_{2}+c_{2}=0, \ n^{\ast}_{1}=-c_{1}, \ n^{\ast}_{2}=-c_{2}</math>
====General exponents, double integral====
This section describes the integration formula for a double integral whose integrand's series expansion may not contain consecutive integer exponents.  [[Matrix (mathematics)|Matrice]]s contain the parameters needed to express the exponents in a series expansion of the integrand, and the [[determinant]] of [[invertible matrix]] <math display="inline"> A</math> is <math display="inline">\det|A|</math>.{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqn. 7}} 
<math display=block>  A= \begin{vmatrix} a_{11} & a_{12} \\ a_{21} & a_{22} \end{vmatrix}, \ C= \begin{vmatrix} c_{1} \\ c_{2} \end{vmatrix}, \  \ N^{\ast}= \begin{vmatrix} n^{\ast}_{1} \\ n^{\ast}_{2} \end{vmatrix}</math>
Applying the substitution <math display=block> y_{1}=x^{a_{11}}_{1} x^{a_{21}}_{2}, \quad y_{2}=x^{a_{12}}_{1} x^{a_{22}}_{2}</math> generates the function series expansion, integral and  integration formula for a double integral whose integrand's series expansion may not contain consecutive integer exponents.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=118}}  The integral and integration formula are{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=118|loc=Eqn. 9.6}}{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqn. 8}} 
<math display=block>  \begin{align}
&\int_0^\infty \int_0^\infty \sum^\infty_{n_{1}=0} \sum^\infty_{n_{2}=0} \frac{(-1)^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!} \frac{(-1)^{n_{2}}}{n_{2}!}  \ \varphi(n_{1},n_{2}) \ x_{1}^{n_{1}a_{11}+n_{2}a_{12}+c_{1}-1}  \ x_{2}^{n_{1}a_{21}+n_{2}a_{22}+c_{2}-1} \ dx_{1} \ dx_{2} \\
&=\det|A|^{-1} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{2}) \ \varphi(n^{\ast}_{1},n^{\ast}_{2}).
\end{align} </math>  The parameter matrix <math display="inline">N^{\ast}</math> is a solution to this linear equation.{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqn. 9}}
<math display=block> AN^{\ast}+C=0, \ N^{\ast}=-A^{-1} C </math>.
====Positive complexity index====
In some cases, there may be more sums than variables.  For example, if the integrand is a product of 3 functions of a common single variable, and each function is converted to a series expansion sum, the integrand is now a product of 3 sums, each sum corresponding to a distinct series expansion. 
*The <em>number of brackets</em> is the number of linear equations associated with an integral.  This term reflects the common practice of bracketing each linear equation.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Kondrashuk|Moll|Recabarren|2022|p=28}}    
* The <em>complexity index</em> is the number of integrand sums minus the number of brackets (linear equations).  Each series expansion of the integrand contributes one sum.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Kondrashuk|Moll|Recabarren|2022|p=28}}  
* The <em>[[Summation|summation indices (variables)]]</em> are the indices that index terms in a series  expansion.  In the example, there are 3 summation indices <math display="inline">n_{1}, n_{2}</math> and <math display="inline">n_{3}</math> because the integrand is a product of 3 series expansions.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=117}}
* The <em>[[Free variables and bound variables|free summation indices (variables)]]</em> are the summation indices that remain after completing all integrations.  Integration reduces the number of sums in the integrand by replacing the series expansions (sums) with an integration formula.  Therefore, there are fewer summation indices after integration. The number of chosen free summation indices equals the complexity index.{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=117}}

====Integrals with a positive complexity index====
The free summation indices <math display="inline">\bar{n}_{1},\ldots, \bar{n}_{f}</math> are elements of set <math display="inline">F</math>.  The matrix of free summation indices is <math display="inline">\bar{N}</math> and the coefficients of the free summation indices is matrix <math display="inline">\bar{A}</math>.
<math display=block>  \bar{A}= \begin{vmatrix} \bar{a}_{11} & \ldots &\bar{a}_{1f} 
\\ \vdots & & \vdots \\
\bar{a}_{b1} & \ldots & \bar{a}_{bf} \end{vmatrix},  \  \bar{N}= \begin{vmatrix} \bar{n}_{1} \\ \vdots \\ \bar{n}_{f} \end{vmatrix}</math>
The remaining indices are set <math display="inline">B</math> containing indices <math display="inline">n_{1},\ldots, n_{b}</math>. 
Matrices  <math display="inline">A, C</math> and <math display="inline">N^{\ast}</math> contain matrix elements that multiply or sum with the non-summation indices.  The selected free summation indices must leave matrix <math display="inline">A</math> non-singular. 
<math display=block>  A= \begin{vmatrix} a_{11} & \ldots &a_{1b} \\ \vdots & & \vdots \\
a_{b1} & \ldots & a_{bb} \end{vmatrix}, \ C= \begin{vmatrix} c_{1} \\ \vdots \\ c_{b} \end{vmatrix}, \  \ N^{\ast}= \begin{vmatrix} n^{\ast}_{1} \\ \vdots \\ n^{\ast}_{b} \end{vmatrix}</math>.  This is the function's series expansion, integral and integration formula.{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqn. 10}}
<math display=block>  \begin{align}
&f(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{b})\\
&=\sum^\infty_{n \in B} \sum^\infty_{\bar{n} \in F}  \frac{(-1)^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!} \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{1}}}{\bar{n}_{1}!}  
\ldots
\frac{(-1)^{n_{b}}}{n_{b}!} \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n_{f}}}}{\bar{n}_{f}!} \varphi(n_{1}, \ldots, n_{b}, \bar{n}_{1}, \dots,  \bar{n}_{f})\prod_{x_{k} \in B} x_{k}^{n_{1}a_{k1}+ \dots + \bar{n}_{1}\bar{a}_{k1}+ \dots + c_{k}-1} \\
&\int^{\infty}_{0} \ldots \int^{\infty}_{0} x^{c_{1}-1} \dots  x^{c_{b}-1} f(x_{1}, \ldots, x_{b})  \ dx_{1} \ldots dx_{b} \\
&=\det|A|^{-1} \sum^\infty_{\bar{n} \in F} \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{1}}}{\bar{n}_{1}!} 
\ldots
\frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{f}}}{\bar{n}_{f}!} 
\ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \ldots \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{b})  \ \varphi(n^{\ast}_{1}, \ldots, n^{\ast}_{b}, \bar{n}_{1}, \dots,  \bar{n}_{f}).
\end{align} </math> 
The parameters <math display="inline">n^{\ast}_{1}, \ldots, n^{\ast}_{b}</math> are linear functions of the  parameters <math display="inline">\bar{n}^{\ast}_{1}, \ldots, \bar{n}^{\ast}_{f}</math>.{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqn. 11}}  
<math display=block>   A \ N^{\ast}+\bar{A} \ \bar{N}+C=0, \ N^{\ast}= -A^{-1}(\bar{A} \ \bar{N}+C)</math>.

===Bracket series===
{| class="wikitable"
|+ Table 1. Bracket series notations
|-
! Notation type !! Power series notation !! Bracket series notation
|-
| Indicator || <math display=block>\frac{(-1)^n}{n !}</math> 
|| <math display=block> \phi_{n} </math>
|-
| Multi-indicator || <math display=block>  \prod_{j=1}^N \left( \frac{(-1)^{n_{j}}}{n_{j}!}  \right) </math>  
|| <math display=block> \phi_{n_1,\ldots ,n_N}</math> 
|-
| Bracket || <math display=block>\int^{\infty}_{0} dx \ x^{a_{1}n_{1}+ \ldots +a_{m}n_{m}+c-1} </math>  
|| <math display=block> \langle a_{1}n_{1}+ \ldots + a_{m}n_{m}+c \rangle </math> 
|}
<em>Bracket series</em> notations are notations that substitute for common power series notations (Table 1).{{sfn|González|Moll|Schmidt|2011|p=8}}   Replacing power series notations with bracket series notations transforms the power series to a bracket series.  A bracket series facilitates identifying the formula parameters needed for integration.  It is also recommended to replace a sum raised to a power:{{sfn|González|Moll|Schmidt|2011|p=8}} <math display=block> \frac{1}{(x_{1}+ \ldots +x_{b})^{\alpha}}</math>
with this bracket series expression:<math display=block>\sum^{\infty}_{m_{1}=0} \ldots \sum^{\infty}_{m_{b}=0} \ \phi_{m_1, \dots,m_b} \ x^{m_{1}}_{1} \dots x^{m_{b}}_{b}\frac{\langle \alpha+m_{1}+ \ldots +m_{b} \rangle}{\Gamma(\alpha)}.</math>

===Algorithm===
This algorithm describes how to apply the integral formulas.{{sfn|Gonzalez|Jiu|Moll|2020|pp=983-985}}{{sfn|Amdeberhan|Gonzalez|Harrison|Moll|2012|p=117|loc=Eqn. 9.5}}{{sfn|Ananthanarayan|Banik|Friot|Pathak|2023|loc=Eqns. 9-11}} 

{| class="wikitable"
|+ Table 2. Integral formulas
|-
! Complexity index !! Integral formula
|-
| Zero, single integral || <math display=block>a^{-1} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast})\,\varphi(n^{\ast})</math>
|-
| Zero, multiple integral || <math display=block>\det |A|^{-1} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \ldots \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{b}) \ \varphi(n^{\ast}_{1}, \ldots, n^{\ast}_{b})</math> 
|-
| Positive || <math display=block>\det |A|^{-1} \sum^\infty_{\bar{n} \in F} \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{1}}}{\bar{n}_{1}!} \ldots \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{f}}}{\bar{n}_{f}!} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \ldots \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{b}) \ 
\varphi(n^{\ast}_{1}, \ldots, n^{\ast}_{b}, \bar{n}_{1}, \dots,  \bar{n}_{f})</math>
|}
:'''Input''' Integral expression
:'''Output''' Integral value or integral cannot be assigned a value
:# Express the integrand as a power series.
:# Transform the integrand's power series to a bracket series.
:# Obtain the complexity index, formula parameters and series coefficient function.
:## Complexity index is the number of integrand sums minus number of brackets.
:## Parameters <math display="inline">n^{\ast}</math> or array <math display="inline">N^{\ast}</math> are solutions to linear equations <math display="inline">an^{\ast}+c=0</math> (zero complexity index, single integral), <math display="inline">AN^{\ast}+C=0</math> (zero complexity index, single integral) or <math display="inline">AN^{\ast}+\bar{A} \bar{N}+C=0</math> (positive complexity index).
:## Identify parameter <math display="inline">a</math> or (zero complexity index, single integral) or compute <math display="inline">\det |A|</math> (all other cases) from the associated linear equations.
:## Identify the series coefficient function <math display="inline">\varphi()</math> of the bracket series.    
:# If the complexity index is negative, return integral cannot be assigned a value.
:# If the complexity index is zero, select the formula from table 2 for zero complexity index,  single or multiple integral, compute the integral value with this formula, and return this integral value.
:# If the complexity index is positive, select the formula from table 2 for positive complexity index, and compute the integral value as a series expansion with this formula for all possible choices of the free summation indices.  Select the lowest complexity index, [[convergent series]] expansion, adding series that converge in the same region.    
:## If all series expansions are divergent series or null series (all series terms zero), then return integral cannot be assigned a value.
:## If the series expansion is non-null and non-divergent, return this series expansion as the integral value.

===Examples===
====Zero complexity index==== 
The bracket method will integrate this integral.  
<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty x^{3/2} \ e^{-x^3/2} \ dx  </math>
<ol>
<li> Express the integrand as a power series.<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n} \ 
 \frac{(-1)^n}{n!} \ x^{(3 \cdot n+5/2)-1} \ dx </math>  </li>
<li>Transform the power series to a bracket series.
<math display=block> \sum_{n=0}^\infty 2^{-n} \ \phi(n) \cdot 
\left \langle 3 \ n+ \frac{5}{2} \right \rangle </math></li>
<li>Obtain the complexity index, formula parameters and series coefficient function.</li>
: Complexity index is zero.
:<math display="inline"> 3 \ n^{\ast}+ 5/2=0</math> 
:<math display="inline"> n^{\ast}= -5/6, \ a=3</math> 
: <math display="inline">\varphi(n)=2^{-n}</math>. 
<li>Use table 2 to compute the integral.</li>
</ol>
<math display=block>  \int_0^\infty x^{3/2} \cdot e^{-x^3/2} \ dx  </math>
<math display=block>  =a^{-1} \ \Gamma(-n^{\ast}) \ \varphi(n^{\ast})</math> 
<math display=block> = \frac{\Gamma \left(\frac{5}{6} \right) \ 2^{5/6}}{3}</math>

====Positive complexity index====
The bracket method will integrate this integral.
<math display=block> \int^{\infty}_{0} \frac{1}{(1+x^{3}+x^{5})^{1/2}} \ dx </math> 
1. Express the integrand as a power series.  Use the sum raised to a power formula.
<math display=block>
\int^{\infty}_{0} \sum_{n_1,n_2,n_3} \ \frac{1}{\sqrt{\Gamma(1/2)}} \phi_{123} 1^{n_{1}} x^{5n_{2}+ 3n_{3}} \langle n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3}+1/2 \rangle \ dx 
</math>
2. Transform the power series to a bracket series. 
<math display=block> \int^{\infty}_{0} \sum_{n_1,n_n,n_3} \frac{1}{\sqrt{\Gamma(1/2)}}  \phi_{123} \langle 5 \ n_{2}+ 3 \ n_{3}+1 \rangle \langle n_{1}+n_{2}+n_{3}+1/2 \rangle  </math>
3. Obtain the complexity index, formula parameters and series coefficient function.
: Complexity index is 1 as 3 sums and 2 brackets.
: Select <math display="inline">n_{3}</math> as the free index, <math display="inline">\bar{n}_{3}</math>.  The linear equations, solutions, determinant and series coefficient are
<math display=block>  5n^{\ast}_{2}+ 3 \bar{n}_{3}+1=0, \  n^{\ast}_{1}+n^{\ast}_{2}+\bar{n}_{3}+1/2=0</math> 
<math display=block>  \begin{vmatrix} 1 & 1 \\ 0 & 5 \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} n^{\ast}_{1} \\ n^{\ast}_{2} \end{vmatrix}
+ \begin{vmatrix} 1 \\ 3 \end{vmatrix} \begin{vmatrix} \bar{n}_{3}\end{vmatrix}+ \begin{vmatrix} 1/2 \\ 1 \end{vmatrix} =0</math> 
<math display=block>  AN^{\ast} + \bar{A} \bar{N} + C =0</math>
<math display=block>  \det |A|=5 </math> 
<math display=block>  n^{\ast}_{1}= -\frac{2}{5} \bar{n}_{3}-\frac{3}{10}, \ n^{\ast}_{2}= -\frac{3}{5} \bar{n}_{3}-\frac{1}{5}.</math> 
<math display=block>  \varphi(n^{\ast}_{1},n^{\ast}_{2}, \bar{n}_{3})= \frac{1}{\sqrt{\Gamma(1/2)}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\pi}} </math>  
4. Use table 2 to compute the integral
<math display=block> \begin{align} 
&\int^{\infty}_{0} \frac{1}{(1+x^{3}+x^{5})^{1/2}} \ dx \\
&=\sum^{\infty}_{\bar{n}_{3}=0} \frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{3}}}{\bar{n}_{3}!} \det |A|^{-1}\Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{1}) \Gamma(-n^{\ast}_{2})
\varphi(n^{\ast}_{1},n^{\ast}_{2},\bar{n}_{3}) \\
&=\sum^{\infty}_{\bar{n}_{3}=0}\frac{(-1)^{\bar{n}_{3}}}{\bar{n}_{3}!} \frac{\Gamma(\frac{2}{5} \bar{n}_{3}+\frac{3}{10})\Gamma(\frac{3}{5} \bar{n}_{3}+\frac{1}{5})}{5 \sqrt{\pi}} 
\end{align} 
</math>
